title: Two usernames that look identical, compare unequal, and both register
assumption: If two strings render the same, they are the same string.

input.display: "Jos\u00e9" (precomposed é, 4 code points) vs "Jose\u0301" (e + combining acute, 5 code points)
input.description: The same visible name typed on two different systems: macOS file APIs and some keyboards produce the decomposed form, most web forms produce the precomposed form.

what_goes_wrong: A uniqueness check with == or a plain UNIQUE index lets both through, so two accounts share one visible name.
why: Unicode allows the same abstract character to be encoded either as one precomposed code point (U+00E9) or as a base letter plus a combining mark (U+0065 U+0301). The two sequences are canonically equivalent, so every renderer draws them identically, but their code points differ and every byte- or code-point comparison says they are different. Normalizing both sides to the same form (NFC or NFD) before comparing or storing makes them equal.

repros.code:
import unicodedata
a = "Jos\u00e9"
b = "Jose\u0301"
print(a == b, len(a), len(b))
print(unicodedata.normalize("NFC", a) == unicodedata.normalize("NFC", b))

fix: Normalize to NFC (or NFKC for identifiers, which also folds compatibility forms) at the boundary where the value enters your system, and store the normalized form; compare normalized forms only.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms

test_cases.note: Your username canonicalizer should map both spellings to the same key.
